Choose Open Settings, turn notifications on for Toskar, and come back.
Update Toskar on your computer to get notifications here
Update Toskar on the computer, then turn notifications on again.
In the car: Toskar needs the microphone and speech recognition
Once you're parked, allow both for Toskar in the phone's privacy settings.
In the car: I didn't catch that
Ask again. If nothing is heard twice in a row, the conversation ends; open Toskar on the car's screen to start again.

sections.title: Reach Toskar away from home
paragraphs: Access from anywhere lets the phones, tablets, and other devices you paired reach Toskar when they're away from home. It's off until you turn it on in API Access. It answers only paired devices' keys, over HTTPS, and only what those devices use: no sign-in page, no settings, and nothing for other apps' keys.

While it's on, Toskar asks your router to open its port (7333 unless you change it), keeps it open, and closes it when you turn access from anywhere off or quit Toskar. The line under the switch says how Toskar can be reached: at the router's address, over IPv6, at an address you entered, through a relay, or why not, such as an internet provider that shares one address among many homes.

If the router won't open a port, there are free ways around it. Forward the port in your router's settings and enter the address it's reached at under Forwarded address. Or use Tailscale: install it here and on your device, and pair the device while both are on Tailscale. The device then reaches Toskar wherever it is, with no port open at all.

When none of that works, Toskar's relay does. Subscribe under Toskar's relay in API Access, for $4.99 a month or $39.99 a year, or in the Toskar app on your phone or tablet. One subscription covers Toskar here and every device paired with it, and it turns on by itself a few seconds after you pay. Manage billing changes the card or cancels; one bought in the app is managed in your device's store.

If your organization runs its own Toskar relay, open Your organization's relay in API Access and enter the relay's name and the enrollment secret your IT team gave you. Toskar then keeps a line open to the relay, so devices get through even when nothing more direct works.

A device takes the most direct way that works: at home first, then directly, then through the relay. Settings on the device shows which. Traffic is encrypted all the way to Toskar, to the certificate the device saved when it was paired, so a router or relay in between can't read it or answer in Toskar's place.
A device paired before access from anywhere learns the way the next time it's home.
steps: Open API Access and turn on Access from anywhere.
Check the line under the switch. If it says Toskar isn't reachable yet, forward the port and enter the address, use Tailscale, subscribe to Toskar's relay, or set up your organization's relay.
Take a paired device off your home Wi-Fi and open Toskar. Its Settings say how it got through.

sections.title: Share Toskar with other people
paragraphs: Everyone in your home or team can use the same Toskar, each with their own chats, memories, files, and automations. Nobody sees anyone else's, not even the Owner. Models, tools, knowledge, and profiles are shared.

Whoever installed Toskar is the Owner and uses it on this computer without signing in. Admins manage models, tools, knowledge, computers, settings, and people other than Admins and the Owner. Members chat and have their own memories and automations. Visitors only chat. Each person sees only the pages their role can use.
Everyone chooses their own App language, the language answers are written in, and Personalization in Settings. Until they do, they have the Owner's.

Who signs in how, from another computer or device: people sign in with their username and password, in any browser. Phones, tablets, watches, and TVs connect with a 6-digit code, under Connect a device. Apps and scripts, such as one using the OpenAI-compatible API, use an API key from API Access. People never need a key. The Owner uses this computer without signing in; to sign in from another device, the Owner makes a sign-in link on People and chooses a password.
Everyone can connect their own phone, tablet, or TV under Settings → Your devices, and disconnect it there. Local network access has to be on first, which an Admin or the Owner turns on.
The People page under Administer lists everyone. Change someone's role there, make them a new password link, or disable them, which signs them out everywhere and stops their keys and automations.
steps: Open People, type the person's name, choose a role, and choose Add.
If local network access is off, choose Turn on network access under the link, so other devices can open it. No API key is needed: the person signs in with a password.
Copy the link and send it to them. It works once, for a week.
They open it, choose a username and password, and are signed in. Next time, they sign in at the same address.
Forgot a password? Choose New password link next to their name and send them the new link.

sections.title: Open a chat page for the people you serve
paragraphs: A chat portal is a page with only a chat on it, in your own name, logo, and colours, for customers, students, or anyone you help. It answers with the profile you choose, and none of Toskar's other pages show.

Each visitor's chats are their own: no other visitor, and none of your own chats, memories, or knowledge sources, appear to them, and their chats never reach your memory or knowledge. A portal starts with no tools and no memory; you can allow tools that only read, or the profile's own.

Each portal has limits: how many messages a visitor may send an hour, how long a message may be, and how many of its chats run at once. Portal chats wait for your own and for other people's who use Toskar, so a busy portal never slows you down.
Turning a portal off under Administer → Portals stops it at once, even for someone in the middle of a chat.

To put a portal on your own website, list the website's address under Embedding in the portal's editor, such as https://shop.example.com, then copy the chat button or the frame snippet onto your pages. Only the websites you list can show it.

Conversations, next to each portal, lists its visitors' chats for you to read, and the portal page tells visitors that the people who run it can read them. Each portal shows how many visitors wrote and how many messages they sent this month, and keeps visitors' chats for the time you choose, 30 days to start. A Members only portal's chats stay each Member's own.
steps: Open Administer → Portals.

Under Add a portal, type a name; the address fills in from it. Choose who can chat: anyone with a passcode you set, anyone on your network, the Members who sign in to this Toskar, or only people you invite. For invited portals, invite each person by name in the portal's editor and send them their link.
Choose the profile, tools, and language, and how it looks: heading, logo, accent colour, theme, welcome message, suggested prompts, and footer. The preview shows the page as visitors will see it.
Copy the link and share it. Local network access has to be on for other devices to open it.

sections.title: Run without a desktop
paragraphs: Extract the matching Linux headless archive and run the daemon from the extracted directory. Keep the bundled web directory alongside it. Open http://127.0.0.1:7331 on that computer.

For a remote server, an SSH tunnel lets you reach the loopback UI: ssh -L 7331:127.0.0.1:7331 user@server. Then open http://127.0.0.1:7331 on your own computer, using a different local port if it is already occupied.

The deb and rpm packages run Toskar as the system service toskar.service (also reachable as yggdrasil.service), as the user yggdrasil, with its data in /var/lib/yggdrasil/.local/share/toskar (.local/share/yggdrasil for an install from before the rename to Toskar). Use systemctl status, restart, and stop, and journalctl -u toskar for its log. The headless archive does not install a service: the daemon accepts --data-dir for a custom data location, and Ctrl+C stops it in a terminal.

config.json in the data directory sets ports, addresses, discovery, and static peers, and TOSKAR_* environment variables override them for containers. The toskarctl command lists, creates, runs, and pauses automations from a terminal, and prints shell completion.

Behind a reverse proxy that signs people in, such as Authelia, Authentik, Cloudflare Access, or Tailscale, set TOSKAR_TRUSTED_PROXIES to the proxy's address. Toskar then takes the person from the proxy's Remote-User header, makes them the first time, and gives them a role from their groups: TOSKAR_PROXY_ADMIN_GROUPS and TOSKAR_PROXY_MEMBER_GROUPS, with TOSKAR_PROXY_DEFAULT_ROLE for everyone else. TOSKAR_PROXY_OWNER_USER is your own name there. Only the listed address is believed. With the proxy on the same computer, everything from that computer counts as the proxy's, so open Toskar through the proxy there too.

To let people sign in with Google, Microsoft, Okta, Authentik, Keycloak, or another OpenID Connect provider, register Toskar there with its address followed by /api/v1/oidc/callback, then set TOSKAR_OIDC_ISSUER, TOSKAR_OIDC_CLIENT_ID, and TOSKAR_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET. The sign-in screen then shows Sign in with that provider. Groups become roles with TOSKAR_OIDC_ADMIN_GROUPS and TOSKAR_OIDC_MEMBER_GROUPS, and TOSKAR_OIDC_OWNER_EMAIL is your own address there.
sections.summary: Run Toskar Core on a computer without a screen, such as a home server, and use it from a browser on your own computer.

blocks.title: What you need
items: A Linux computer you can sign in to from a terminal, with Toskar Core installed. [Install and start your first chat](#install) has the install script and the apt lines.
Memory and disk space for a model, as on any computer. The same table on that page applies.
Your own computer, with a browser and SSH, to use it from.

blocks.text: The service

The Linux packages run Toskar as the system service toskar, which starts when the computer does. It runs as the user yggdrasil, and keeps its data in /var/lib/yggdrasil/.local/share/toskar. Install the packages with sudo, since they set up the service.
Check it, restart it, or read its log with systemd's usual commands. These need a Linux computer with the service, so they aren't run in CI.

blocks.code:
systemctl status toskar
sudo systemctl restart toskar
journalctl -u toskar

blocks.text: Open Toskar from your own computer
At first, Toskar answers only on the server itself, at 127.0.0.1:7331. An SSH tunnel brings that address to your own computer, and nothing is opened to the network.

items: On your own computer, open a terminal and run ssh -L 7331:127.0.0.1:7331 you@server, with your username and the server's name. Leave it open.
Open http://127.0.0.1:7331 in a browser on your own computer.
The first time, set up a model as on any computer: choose what you'd like your AI to do, then Install recommended setup.

blocks.text: Through the tunnel, Toskar answers as it would on the server. This check, from your own computer, shows that it's running:
If your own computer runs Toskar too, 7331 is taken there. Use another port on your side, such as ssh -L 7400:127.0.0.1:7331 you@server, and open http://127.0.0.1:7400.
You're the Owner

Whoever installed Toskar is its Owner, and uses it from the server without signing in. A tunnel arrives as the server, so you're the Owner through it too. To add other people, or to sign in from another device, see [People and sign-in](#people).
Update

Once a day, Toskar asks toskar.ai for the latest version number, and nothing else. When there's a newer one, Settings shows it under About, such as Toskar 1.13.0 is available. Update the way you installed:

rows: The apt repository, or the install script on Debian or Ubuntu
`sudo apt-get update`, then `sudo apt-get upgrade`
An rpm package
The new release's rpm, with `sudo dnf install` and its file name
Homebrew
`brew upgrade toskar`

blocks.text: Running the install script again doesn't update: it says Toskar is already installed and running. A Linux package restarts the service on the new version by itself.
Settings for a server

config.json in the data directory sets ports, addresses, discovery, and static peers, and TOSKAR_* environment variables override them for containers. The toskarctl command lists, creates, runs, and pauses automations from a terminal, and prints shell completion.
The headless archive doesn't install a service. Extract it, run toskar from its folder with the web folder beside it, and stop it with Ctrl+C. Its --data-dir option keeps the data somewhere else.
Sign in through a proxy or your organization's accounts

Behind a reverse proxy that signs people in, such as Authelia, Authentik, Cloudflare Access, or Tailscale, set TOSKAR_TRUSTED_PROXIES to the proxy's address. Toskar then takes the person from the proxy's Remote-User header, makes them the first time, and gives them a role from their groups: TOSKAR_PROXY_ADMIN_GROUPS and TOSKAR_PROXY_MEMBER_GROUPS, with TOSKAR_PROXY_DEFAULT_ROLE for everyone else. TOSKAR_PROXY_OWNER_USER is your own name there. Only the listed address is believed. With the proxy on the same computer, everything from that computer counts as the proxy's, so open Toskar through the proxy there too.

To let people sign in with Google, Microsoft, Okta, Authentik, Keycloak, or another OpenID Connect provider, register Toskar there with its address followed by /api/v1/oidc/callback, then set TOSKAR_OIDC_ISSUER, TOSKAR_OIDC_CLIENT_ID, and TOSKAR_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET. The sign-in screen then shows Sign in with that provider. Groups become roles with TOSKAR_OIDC_ADMIN_GROUPS and TOSKAR_OIDC_MEMBER_GROUPS, and TOSKAR_OIDC_OWNER_EMAIL is your own address there.
Troubleshooting

rows: The browser can't reach 127.0.0.1:7331
Check that the tunnel's terminal is still open. On the server, `systemctl status toskar` says whether Toskar is running.
bind: Address already in use, when you start the tunnel
Something on your own computer has port 7331. Use another port on your side, as in the tip above.
The service stopped after an update
`journalctl -u toskar` shows why. Restart it with `sudo systemctl restart toskar`.
Settings doesn't say when there's an update
The update check is off, or the server can't reach toskar.ai. Turn on Check for updates under About.

sections.title: Privacy, encryption, and what left this computer
paragraphs: Are my chats private? Yes. Your chats, memories, knowledge, and files stay on this computer. Only people who can sign in to your account on it, and apps you give an API key, can see them; a chat answered by one of your paired computers is sent to that computer. There is no Toskar account or cloud, and nobody at Toskar can see your chats or data.

Toskar does not send usage telemetry. Chats, memories, knowledge, files, and specialized AIs are stored in the data directory on this computer. Something leaves only when a feature that goes online is used: a web search or page read, a connected service or MCP server, a database or web API you connected, a model or runtime download, a paired computer that answers a chat or trains, or an external server you configured.

Settings → What left this computer lists each of those, newest first: the search queries, page addresses, what was sent to a paired computer or an external server, and what a connected service was asked. It counts them for the last 30 days.

Run records hold the prompts and tool results of past runs, including that list. Keep run records for sets how long they are kept: 7, 30, or 90 days, or Keep them. Delete run records now removes them at once, and clears cached web searches and pages. Chats are not run records; History in Settings decides whether chats are saved.

Memories and knowledge sources marked This computer only keep every chat that uses them on this computer. Text recognition, meaning search, and training on this computer never send your data elsewhere.

Is my data encrypted? Toskar doesn't encrypt its own files, and encryption isn't required to use it. Turn on your computer's disk encryption to keep chats, memories, knowledge, and files encrypted while the computer is off or locked: FileVault on macOS (System Settings → Privacy & Security), BitLocker or Device Encryption on Windows, and LUKS on Linux. Passwords and keys for connected services are kept in the secrets folder, readable only by your user account.

Websites, model downloads, and online services are reached over encrypted HTTPS connections. Addresses you enter yourself, such as an external server, a webhook, or an MCP server, are encrypted when they start with https://. Traffic between your own paired computers, and from other devices on your network to this computer (local network access), is not encrypted yet; it is protected by pairing and API keys, so use those features on a network you trust, such as your home or office network. Settings → Your data stays private sums this up.

sections.title: Settings and storage
paragraphs: Settings controls appearance, the default profile, where chats run, model lifecycle and storage, downloads, notifications, history, tool permissions, personalization, and what left this computer. Finding other computers and the external server are on the Computers page, and connected services are on the Tools page. The sidebar groups pages into Use (Chat, Automations, Knowledge, Memory), Customize (Models, Tools, Profiles & Orchestration), and Administer (Train, Computers, API Access, Performance, Diagnostics), with Settings at the bottom. Administer is closed until you open it. Advanced mode shows expert controls inside pages: editing profiles, per-tool permissions, and run details under answers. Desktop settings also keep Toskar running in the background and launch it at login. Saving an automation's schedule turns on Keep running in background, because schedules stop when the daemon stops.

Personalization shapes how answers look in every chat, automation, and API request: length (brief, balanced, or detailed), tone (friendly, neutral, or direct), format (prose or lists), units (metric or imperial), and two short notes, about you and how to answer. It never changes what tools may do.

Default data locations are ~/Library/Application Support/Toskar on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Toskar on Windows, and ~/.local/share/toskar on Linux. An install from before the rename keeps its Yggdrasil folder (yggdrasil on Linux), and nothing is moved. Settings shows the actual data, model, runtime, and log directories. SQLite state, model files, and runtime files live under the data tree.

Before replacing an installation or resetting the app, stop the app and daemon and back up the data directory if you need its state. Review the reset dialog carefully. Install updates from the matching release archive and restart the app.

sections.title: Diagnostics and performance
paragraphs: Diagnostics shows the health of the control service, the model runtime, the database, networking, storage, and the API, with a plain status for each. What Toskar can do lists every ability, such as looking things up, reading files, or training, with how it works or what would make it possible. Chat answers questions like “Can you generate an image?” from the same list. Tool activity shows recent tool calls. Export diagnostics writes a troubleshooting bundle without secrets.

Performance shows what your AI is doing right now and recent runs with their speed. Compare models runs the same benchmark on several models, and Recent benchmarks keeps the results. In advanced mode, Run details under an answer shows how it was handled: the models and computers used, load time, time to first token, tokens per second, tool calls, and retries.

sections.title: Is my model using the GPU?
sections.summary: See whether a model runs on your graphics card, why it doesn't when it could, and how to fix that.
paragraphs: A model answers much faster on a graphics card (GPU) than on the processor (CPU). Toskar shows where each running model actually runs, as llama.cpp reported when it loaded the model, not what the hardware could do.

blocks.title: What you need
items: A running model. Sending a chat message starts one.

blocks.text: Where to look

Each running model shows a status on Models › Running and on the Performance overview. Select it to see the device, how many of the model's layers are on the GPU, and the GPU memory it uses. Diagnostics has a GPU acceleration row with the same states.

blocks.alt: The Running tab with Gemma 4 E4B running on this Mac, marked GPU in green
blocks.caption: GPU, in green: the whole model is on the graphics card.

rows: GPU (green)
The whole model is on the graphics card.
Partly on GPU (amber)
It doesn't fit in the GPU's memory, so some of it runs on the slower CPU. A smaller model, or a smaller version of this one, fits completely.
CPU only (red)
This computer has a GPU that isn't being used. The steps below fix it.
CPU (grey)
This computer has no GPU Toskar can use, which is expected.

blocks.text: A model bigger than your graphics card still runs. Toskar puts as many of its layers as fit in the card's free memory there, and the rest in the computer's memory, where the processor runs them, so it shows Partly on GPU. A mixture-of-experts model, such as one marked A3B, keeps its experts in the computer's memory first, since each word uses only a few of them. In Toskar 1.11 and earlier, a model that didn't fit on the card stopped while loading instead.
Watch it live

The Performance overview shows each computer's CPU and memory, and each graphics card's use, video memory, temperature, and power, with the last hour as a line. Activity marks each reply GPU or CPU and can filter by it. With Advanced mode on, a reply's details also say how many words the model guessed ahead and how many it kept, and Activity shows the share kept across the replies shown; filter by a model to see its own. More kept means faster answers.
A Mac doesn't report GPU temperature or power without administrator rights, and Windows reports them only for NVIDIA cards. Toskar leaves those figures out there rather than showing zero.
Troubleshooting
When a model shows CPU only:

items: If a model shows CPU only, open Diagnostics and read the reason under GPU acceleration.
If the installed llama.cpp runs on the CPU only, stop your models, then quit and reopen Toskar. It installs the GPU build when no model is running.

If llama.cpp couldn't use the GPU, install or update the graphics driver. On Linux with an AMD or Intel card, also install the Vulkan drivers (on Ubuntu and Debian, mesa-vulkan-drivers and libvulkan1).
Start the model again and check its status.

sections.title: Why do answers in a long chat start slowly?
sections.summary: See how much of a chat each model skips reading again, and what to do when one reads it all every turn.
paragraphs: Before a model answers, it reads the whole chat so far. On a chat's later turns, it can skip the part it already read, kept in its prompt cache, and read only your new message. A model that can't skip reads a long chat from the start every turn, so its answers start later as the chat grows.

blocks.title: What you need
items: A few chats of more than one turn from the last week, with models running on this computer.

blocks.text: Where to look
Open Diagnostics. Reusing the chat so far lists each model with the share of its later turns' prompts it skipped, and how many turns and tokens that covers.

blocks.alt: Diagnostics listing Gemma 4 E4B at 92% skipped and Qwen Coder 7B at 10%, marked low
blocks.caption: Gemma 4 E4B skipped 92% of what it had read before; Qwen Coder 7B is marked low.

rows: 80% or more
Normal. Each turn reads little more than your new message.
Low, under 50%
Over at least five turns, the model read most of each chat again. Its answers slow down as a chat grows.
No panel
No chat had a second turn this week, or your models ran on another computer or app, which don't report this.

blocks.text: Only turns after a chat's first are counted, and only when the model was already running. A model that just started has nothing to skip. Models on paired computers and in other apps, such as Ollama, don't report it, so they aren't listed.
Toskar's weekly tests hold a small model to 80% or more, and check that an answer from the cache matches one read from scratch, word for word.
Troubleshooting
When a model is marked low:

items: Switch between chats less while you wait for answers. Each chat you send to the same model can push the others out of its cache.
Try a different model for long chats. Some models, such as those with sliding-window attention, can't skip as much.
Let a long chat be shortened. Auto-compact summarizes older turns, so there's less to read again.
If a model stays low, report it from Diagnostics, so Toskar can tune how it runs that model.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
paragraphs: Start with What I did under the answer: it names the model that answered and why, and what went wrong. No reply or a model load failure: confirm the installation finished, check the selected computer is online, close memory-heavy applications, or try a smaller model. A model that cannot load fails at once with the reason.

No live web answer: check that Internet is allowed in the profile, and ask for a search or about something current; a plain question is answered without tools. The same search within 15 minutes is answered from the cache.

An answer did not use your knowledge or memories: use Try a question on the Knowledge page, install an embedding model so search matches meaning, and check that memory is on for the chat. A knowledge source that failed shows the reason; database and web API sources keep answering from the last data fetched.

API connection refused: confirm the daemon is running and copy the current endpoint from API Access. A 401 with local network access on means a request from an app on another device needs a valid API key (people signing in in a browser use their password instead), and a 403 means the key does not allow what the request asked for. Run Test API after changing settings.

To tell the Toskar team about a problem, use Report this beside the error (see Report a problem). For the public issue tracker, include the app version, OS and processor, model, profile, steps to reproduce, and relevant diagnostics, and remove secrets and private prompt or file content before posting.

sections.title: Report a problem
paragraphs: Most errors have Report this beside them: in the app and the desktop app, on the phone and tablet, and on the TV. It opens the report so you see everything it sends before it goes, with room to say what you were doing. Nothing is sent until you send it.

A report says what went wrong and where: the error and its code, the page or screen, the app and its version, and the device's system. When you're connected to a computer, it adds that computer's Toskar version, its operating system, processor, memory, and graphics. An Admin's report also has the computer's last 40 warnings and errors from its log; a Member's doesn't, and a Visitor's leaves out the computer entirely.

Before you see it, the report has email addresses, keys and tokens, and the name in home-folder paths taken out, and internet addresses replaced by their kind, such as public IPv4; the computer's part also has the computer's name taken out. Addresses on your home network stay, since they help and say nothing about where you are, and so do IDs that match the report to a log. Read it before sending; take out anything else you'd rather not share.

In the app and the desktop app, Send gives the report to the Toskar team through your computer, and it becomes an issue they can fix, kept private. If others hit the same error in the same version, yours is added to theirs, and the report says so. Include details, on unless you turn it off, adds the computer's part; an email address you add, for a reply, goes only to the Toskar team, never into the issue. Each report sent is listed in What left this computer.

When it can't be sent that way, such as with no internet connection, Send by email opens your own email app with the same report to info@yeix.io, and you can always choose Or send it by email instead. The phone, tablet, and TV send by email for now. A long report drops its oldest log lines to fit in an email.

The TV has no email app, so its report shows a code: scan it with your phone's camera and the email opens there. On the watch, Report on phone hands the problem to the phone, and the report shows the next time you open Toskar there.

Toskar doesn't send reports, crash data, or usage data on its own. A report leaves only when you send it, and only what it showed you. An Admin can turn off sending reports to Toskar in Settings, under Problem reports; then Report this only copies the report, to give to whoever runs Toskar.
To report an answer rather than a problem, such as a wrong or offensive one, use Report this answer under it on the phone or tablet. It works the same way: your email app opens with the report.
